articles.text: Thursday, October 30, will be the last chance to visit the Wildwood Dads Club’s Pumpkin Patch in the Coaches Field parking lot. The patch has enjoyed record-breaking sales this year and was restocked Tuesday morning for one final pumpkin-purchasing hurrah. On Sunday, October 26, the patch had its best sales day in history, with pumpkins flying out the gates destined for Piedmont stoops, patios, dining tables and porches. “We’ve seen a ton of community support. I was out there for at least three hours [Sunday] and just kept unloading pallet after pallet. People kept buying, and I kept putting them out there; it’s a virtuous cycle,” said “Patch Papa” Mike Hagerty. Hagerty said it wasn’t just the kids who were excited about the orange gourds, everyone involved showed enthusiasm. “I went to someone’s house with a pumpkin display, and they were describing how much they liked each variety. ‘I like this color, this shape, and this one for pumpkin pie,’” said Hagerty. In addition to hundreds of volunteer hours logged by Wildwood parents and their kids, the Patch’s success is also thanks in part to longtime pumpkin vendor Kevin from Fuji Melons. articles.text: The 13th Annual Artisanal Piedmont Beer Festival drew a full crowd to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, October 24, as local brewers poured their best pilsners, ales, IPAs, and more for a night of community, creativity, and flavor. Guests enjoyed an Oktoberfest-style meal on the lawn, donated and served by Piedmont Grocery, while a trio of Piedmont High musicians provided live music to set the evening’s relaxed tone. A total of 22 craft beers were available for tasting — from lighter pilsners to high-ABV “barley wines” and inventive blends such as prickly pear and passion fruit. “I don’t know what I love more, hanging out with the people who are brewing or serving the residents of Piedmont,” said brewer Michael Fedor, participating for the second time this year. His Piedmont Pala Ave Pale Ale, brewed with home-grown hops, took home awards for both Crowd Favorite and Best Ale. Judges for the evening included Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson, City Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, Nancy Kent, Steve Roland, and Don Ashburn, who deliberated on five award categories: • Best Ale – Piedmont Pala Avenue Pale Ale • Most Unusual – Grapeful Dead • Best Specialty Beer – Yerba Mate Hazy IPA • Crowd Favorite – Piedmont Pala Avenue Pale Ale • Best in Show – Eddy’s Ale Many small-batch brews sported playful names, such as Jon Rhodin’s 9% ABV barley wine MOJO—a robust, hop-forward creation. “With the high [alcohol] percentage beers, you can get really creative,” said brewer Ed Sweeney. “You can do all different additives, you can use different hops, more hops, more malts, Ed Sweeney (left) and Case Gardner of Highland Brewing won Best in Show for their English Special Bitter, titled Eddy’s Ale.

articles.text: Witches took shelter under every Piedmont Avenue stoop on Saturday, October 25, as a cast of more water-impervious ghouls and goblins braved the open streets and the dubious drizzles, sprinkles and rain. The wet weather did not stop many hundreds of Halloween revelers from enjoying the 38th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade and Costume Contest and all the Avenue has to offer. The parade was led by bagpiper David Winter celebrating the fall classic as trick or treaters got an early sweet taste of the usual autumnal bounty. Costumes were the rule, not the exception making the parade a wet and wild trip through the streets. At Fenton’s, kids lined up by the bucketful for a taste of a free pumpkin ice cream chocked full of cookies. Most store fronts opened their doors to every sort of furry creature a cat could drag in for trick or treating. The Piedmont Avenue Elementary School opened up its playground and installed bouncy houses, and carnival games. It was a sight to see and the place to be especially in the front courtyards of restaurants bordering the Avenue. Kids didn’t have to walk far to fill their buckets to the brim. Families in strollers tossed their cares to the wind, as wet pancake stacks of cardboard and giant egg costumes braved through the afternoon, solidified by the most important meal of the day. Dogs dressed up in fitting shapes and getups as well with wings and headturning tutus. articles.text: Kiki is a confident, clever, and athletic 3-year-old with big, expressive eyes and a purr that rarely stops. This curious girl loves to play – especially with fishing-line wand toys. Her graceful leaps are as impressive as her enthusiasm. She’s so proud of her catches that she’ll sometimes drag the whole wand away like a trophy. A quick learner, Kiki already knows some clicker training and would love to keep showing off her smarts. She’s also a fan of running water and may join you at the sink for a sip while you brush your teeth. Kiki enjoys affection on her own terms. She might let you know with a gentle swat when she’s ready for a break, so she’ll do best in a calm, adultonly home with adopters who appreciate her bold, independent streak. articles.text: The Cancer League’s annual Black & White Holly Ball Gala will return Friday, December 5 at the Claremont Country Club. articles.text: How can my child stay connected while avoiding the potential danger and brainrot of a smartphone? We’ve heard this question often. “It will be many years before I want to give my child a smartphone, but she wants to be able to plan her own hangouts like I did when I was a kid,” says Havens mom and Piedmont Unplugged co-founder Melissa Partovi. Old-fashioned flipphones work for some kids and are available from mobile service providers for a modest monthly fee. But some newer options likewise let your child contact friends and family with fewer pitfalls than a smartphone: “The Landline for Kids” — Tin Cans • Tin Cans let even young kids make calls on an internet-enabled landline. Version 1.0 plugs into an ethernet port; a forthcoming model is wifi-enabled. • Calling other Tin Cans is free; a plan that lets kids interact with other pre-approved numbers is $9.99/month. • Why we like it: Kids can chat like it’s 1989…and that’s it. • Some Piedmont families already plan to implement Tin Can clusters: “I ordered three–one for my kids, two for their best friends,” says Brooke Wall, mom of two Beach students. “Several other families in my son’s grade have ordered them, too.” • www.tincan.kids. • Join the Piedmont Unplugged mailing list and receive a discount code with our next newsletter. The Dumb Smartphone — Gabb 4 • The Gabb 4 is a locked-down Android phone without internet, social media, or games. • Kids can call and text pre-approved numbers. There is a camera, plus optional Maps, Weather, and music-streaming. For parents, there is GPS tracking and a portal to approve contacts. • Why we like it: Has the looks and some of the fun features of a smartphone with fewer downsides. “My fifth-grader has a Gabb 4. It can be a little wonky but she loves being able to talk with her friends and to tell me where she is heading after school.” –Amanda. • Around $150; plans range from $25-35 per month. • Gabb now offers a locked-down smartwatch as well. • www.gabb.com. Slimmed-Down Smartphones • The Gabb 4 Pro, Pinwheel, Troomi, and Bark allow calling and texts with some internet access. These may be suitable for young teens because they allow parents to control the choice of apps–for example, to exclude social media like Snap and TikTok. • Most have parent portals enabling time limits on apps and bedtime shutoff. • Why we like them: These are transitional products for older kids who want to use a few choice apps–but they offer fewer potential loopholes where kids can circumvent restrictions than regular smartphones. Can I Lock Down an iPhone? • Parents can implement controls on an iPhone, such as time limits and restricting App Store downloads, by creating a “Family Sharing” phone group and following the instructions on Apple’s website. • Unfortunately, kidproofing a fully functional product means removing features rather than adding only what you want, which makes it easy to miss loopholes kids can learn about and exploit. • Apple Watches face similar issues. And Android phones may be even more difficult to fully lock down than iPhones. • In sum: Better than an unfettered smartphone, but less protective than some alternatives. For more ideas and smart-phone-free strategies for kids, visit www.PiedmontUnplugged.org.

articles.text: Over the extended weekend of October 11-13, fifteen Piedmont Scouts and six adults from Troop 15 camped at Upper Pines Campground in Yosemite Valley. Ten Scouts proceeded to hike to the top of El Capitan, a long 17-mile day hike with 5,000 feet of elevation gain. The hike to the summit of El Capitan began in the dark, at 6 a.m. with 13 Scouts. The first few miles were brisk and cold, climbing up switchbacks with tough terrain. After many hours of ascending the team made it to the first milestone, the top of Yosemite Falls. Three Scouts turned back after reaching the top of Yosemite Falls while a group of ten continued to the top of El Cap. Scouts made it to the summit after nine miles of grueling uphill climbing, full of switchbacks, rocky terrain, insane views, burning legs, and grit. From the peak, hikers could see Half Dome down below in the background. At the summit the group took a lunch break and fueled up to descend the mountain back into Yosemite Valley. Pictured on El Cap are Scouts Gabriel Topete (left), Caleb Canada, Trenton Downing, Ben Gitter, Ganden Deming, Rory Hull, Max Schultz, Finely Muthig, Camille Hauser, Victoria Mbise and adult leader Regina O’Connor (back). The group back at camp spent their day around the campsite testing their fishing skills. Once the summit group returned to camp, they shared tales from their journey around a campfire while eating the catch of the day. After the descent, the adventure was capped off closer to sea level with a walk around Yosemite’s El Capitan Meadows before returning home. From the summit of El Capitan Piedmont scouts look at the top of Half Dome Scouts caught a trout while fishing, then proceeded to clean it and cook it. Henry Ciriacruz grills it over the campfire. Victoria Mbise (left), Kaleb Costello, and Camille Hauser at an amazing viewpoint of Yosemite Valley Yosemite Falls is down to a trickle in October, long after the springtime snow melt and before the winter rains. On the way out of Yosemite, Scouts took a walk around El Capitan Meadows. Pictured are Leo Thakur (left), Mia Thakur, Sudheer Thakur, Stacy Readal, Victoria Mbise, Kaleb Costello, Regina O’Connor, Rory Hull, Ganden Deming, Ben Gitter, and Max Schultz.

articles.text: Staff Photos Samantha Huyhn (left) and Emma Chan clinched Piedmont’s 4-3 win over Alameda at No. 1 doubles. They were the last match of the day. Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team captured the 2025 Western Alameda County Conference’s title in a dramatic way. Playing league rival Alameda on Wednesday, October 22 at home, they won 4-3 capped by a remarkable victory by the No. 1 doubles team of Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan. In the last match of the day and the teams tied at 3-3, the PHS tandem lost the first set 6-2 and trailed 3-0 in the second set. Mounting a remarkable comeback, they won the second set in a 7-6 (7-2) tiebreak, then won the third set 10-5 for the team victory. They won 5-2 over Berkeley the next day, October 23, at the Berkeley Tennis Club and clinched the title by beating Bishop O’Dowd at home 5-2 on Tuesday, October 28. (Final scores were not reported by press time.)It marks the school’s first title banner since 2022. Against Alameda, it all came down to No. 1 doubles team Samantha Huyhn and Emma Chan with the match deadlocked at 3-3. After losing the first set 6-2 and trailing 3-0 in the second set, the duo mounted a huge comeback to win the second set in a 7-6 (7-2) tiebreak, then winning the third set 10-5 for the team victory. “We were down 3-0 and brought it up to 4-3, then 5-all and 6-all. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team qualified for North Coast Section for the first time since 2018. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team closed its regular season with a 3-0 loss to Castro Valley at Binks Rawlings Gym on Wednesday, October 22 and a 3-1 loss at Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, October 24. However, though finishing its season with a 9-11 overall record, the Highlanders qualified for the Division 4 North Coast Section for the first time since 2018. PHS enters the playoffs as the No. 8 seed and will play No. 9 Urban of San Francisco today, October 29. Piedmont beat the Blues 3-1 earlier this season on September 9. Wednesday’s postseason match marks the school’s first time hosting a playoff game since 2017 when the Highlanders were the No. 7 seed, but lost to No. 10 St. Patrick 3-2. If Piedmont beats Urban, it will mark the school’s first NCS win since 2015, when the school upset No. 8 St. Helena 3-0. “We qualified for NCS, it’s the first time in I don’t even know how long. We are getting good talent coming in. Volleyball is really becoming a staple kind of sport and everyone is interested in it,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Although Piedmont’s losses brought their league record to 2-8, each set against Castro Valley was separated by fewer than seven points. “The underclassmen are ready for it. They just need another club season and they’ll be ready for next year. It’s been a long time. We knew we’d have rocky moments, but the program is building, we should be even better next year,” Cardenas said. Piedmont celebrated its two members from the Class of 2026 for Senior Night prior to the match, Stella Wilk and Mira Sachs. “I’ve been with Stella and Mira since they were freshmen,” Cardenas explained. I coached them on JV all the way through varsity. Stella has been a really good leader on and off the court. Mira has always been really, really kind. They both show their leadership in different ways, “ 3-0 to Castro Valley Piedmont lost by narrow scores of 25-23, 25-18, 25-19. In the first set, both teams traded the early points before Piedmont scored four straight to take an 8-7 lead. However, CV got back to the front at 9-8 and never relinquished. Piedmont tied the set at 14-14 after two straight kills by Maika Ting, while PHS trailed 22-21. CV closed the set with a winning kill. Castro Valley controlled the second set, opening with a 10-2 lead. Piedmont clawed back late, scoring seven of nine points to put them back 24-18, but a service error won it for the Trojans. It was similar in the third set with the Trojans going up 17-7 at one point. PHS fought to keep itself within distance at 23-18, but Stella Wilk goes up for a spike. Piedmont honored her on Senior Night before playing Castro Valley.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country team competed in two different events over the past week. They recently ran at the Haystack Tune-Up Invitational at Hayward High on Saturday, October 25 and the Mid-Season Mania 3200 Invitational at Campolindo in Moraga three days earlier on Wednesday, October 22. At the event in Hayward, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed second of nine schools while the boys’ team was fifth of 14 teams. PHS brought eight athletes to the 3200 invitational at Campolindo. “The varsity girls’ team raced well on Saturday, besting every team except for College Preparatory, who scored just 56 points. Each of the girls ran a solid race. Again, the boys keep getting better and stronger with each passing week. While not everyone was at the top of their game on Saturday, they are still fit and strong and can race well, and we are getting them ready to compete at their best and be ready for the showdown at NCS on November 22,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Leighton Mand placed eighth of 71 runners at the Haystack Tune-Up and 42nd at the MidSeason Mania. Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team placed fifth out of 14 schools at the Haystack Tune-Up. Pictured are Devon Thai (left), Alex Schleuning, Noah Sohn, Dresden Schulte-Sasse, Ian Chung, Aaron Bennett, and Dylan Wallway. Leighton Mand led the girls’ team in Hayward, placing eighth of 71 runners in 19:06.87 on the three-mile course. She was also 42nd of 127 at the Mid-Season Mania. “I wanted to start the race not pushing the first mile, but keeping decent positioning, and focusing on what I can do throughout the entire race instead of just getting out hard. articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), the oldest independent youth orchestra in California, opens its 89th season with a fall concert on Saturday, Nov. 8, at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The performance features a dynamic program that includes Hector Berlioz’s Le Corsaire Overture, Maurice Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole, and Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8. “This concert highlights the talents of our young musicians and introduces YPSO’s new season,” said Executive Director Nadia Liu. “As we look ahead to our international tour, we are excited to share these performances with our community.” The evening opens with Berlioz’s Le Corsaire, an energetic overture known for its dramatic flair and vivid orchestration. Ravel’s Rapsodie Espagnole follows, showcasing Spanish-inspired rhythms and textures. The concert concludes with Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, celebrated for its pastoral warmth and expressive melodies. The orchestra, composed of musicians aged 12 to 22, continues its tradition of offering professional-level performance opportunities while fostering musical education and growth. YPSO enters the new season with a focus on musical excellence and community engagement. The 2025-26 season includes a celebration of the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States and culminates in an international tour scheduled for June 2026. Music Director David Ramadanoff has led YPSO for over three decades. He studied at the Cleveland Institute of Music and The Juilliard School, before serving as Assistant Conductor of the San Francisco Symphony. Maestro Ramadanoff chooses programs that “highlight diverse eras and composers while fostering each student’s musical growth.” Tickets for the Nov. 8 concert are available through YPSO’s website and at the door. For more information, visit ypso.org. The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra is composed of talented musicians aged 12 to 22.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present the world premiere of The Monkey King, a new opera by composer Huang Ruo and librettist David Henry Hwang. Performances will be from November 14 to 30 at the War Memorial Opera House. The production is an adaptation of Journey to the West, the 16th-century Chinese novel attributed to Wu Cheng’en. The opera follows Sun Wukong, the mythical Monkey King, on his quest for immortality and enlightenment, blending elements of opera, dance and puppetry. The Monkey King is “Asia’s supreme superhero, loved and adored not only by Chinese people throughout the centuries but increasingly by people throughout the world,” Ruo said in a press release. “The Monkey King’s adventures awaken in him an understanding of true power which leads to his self-enlightenment,” he said. “In our new opera, which blends cultural traditions with a spectacular multidisciplinary production, I hope to bring this Eastern superhero to life and shine a positive light that will always appear in any turbulent time.” Conductor Carolyn Kuan, music director of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra, makes her San Francisco Opera debut leading the new work. The production is directed by Diane Paulus, artistic director of the American Repertory Theater, with puppetry by Basil Twist, choreography by Composer Huang Ruo Ann Yee, and designs by Anita Yavich, Ayumu “Poe” Saegusa, and Hana S. Kim. Australian-Chinese tenor Kang Wang debuts with the company as the titular Monkey King. The cast also includes soprano Mei Gui Zhang as Guanyin, tenor Konu Kim as the Jade Emperor, bass Peixin Chen as Supreme Sage Laojun, and baritone Joo Won Kang in dual roles as Dragon King Ao Guang and Lord Erlang. Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said the production continues the company’s tradition of “building cultural bridges across the Pacific Ocean.” He called The Monkey King “a stunning and magical undertaking” and said the company hopes it will “become a beloved and lasting opera for the world.” The Monkey King will be performed in English and Mandarin with English and Chinese supertitles. Eight performances are scheduled between Nov. 14 and 30. Tickets and information are available at www.sfopera.com.
articles.title: San Francisco Opera premieres The Monkey King Nov. 14

articles.text: Tickets are on sale now for San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite Nutcracker. The production runs from December 5 to 28. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers within the company to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. The company’s former artistic director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by a live orchestra that performs Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. The San Francisco Chronicle named Nutcracker one of Tomasson’s “finest achievements.” A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older, no children under the age of three will be permitted. Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. A sensory-friendly performance will be held on December 28. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker/. Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker begins December 5. articles.text: Exhibition leaves Nov. 30 The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) presents Routed West: Twentieth-Century African American Quilts in California, an exhibition of more than one hundred quilts by approximately eighty artists, on view now through November 30. African American Quilts is the most expansive presentation to date of a transformative bequest of African American quilts that BAMPFA received in 2019, and highlights the history of the Second Great Migration where African Americans emigrated from the south fleeing economic and racial oppression. Many families settled in California, bringing quiltmaking traditions from the communities they had left behind. Approximately one fourth of the quilts displayed were completed in the South prior to 1950, while others were created in California during the postwar era. Also featured in the exhibition are nearly a dozen recent artworks by Black quilt artists in the Bay Area, including members of the African American Quilt Guild of Oakland. Curator Elaine Yau, a distinguished folk art specialist who has overseen the collection since 2019, said the exhibition highlights BAMPFA’s multi-year initiative to research, catalog, and conserve the nearly three thousand African American quilts and several hundred unattributed quilts in its care. The exhibition is believed to comprise the largest collection of its kind, according to museum officials. “With Routed West, we’re activating the extraordinary collection of African American quilts at BAMPFA to honor the stories of the individuals and communities whose vibrant artistic traditions are indispensable to, but too often omitted from, the larger narrative of American art history, and of our own history here in California,” Yau said in a press release. “These magnificent quilts carry within them stories of resilience, creativity, self-determination, and ingenuity, [including] narratives that not only define a distinctive period of artistic production but also inform a deeper understanding of the intergenerational ties that continue to sustain Black life in the United States,” she added. The exhibition is on view through November 30, Wednesdays through Sundays, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. For more information about this exhibition and BAMPFA’s summer season, visit bampfa.org.
articles.title: Last chance to see African American Quilts at BAMPFA

articles.text: Black Gold: Stories Untold leaves Fort Point National Historic Site in the Presidio this Sunday, November 2. The exhibition highlights the transformative impact of Black communities on California’s cultural, social, and political worlds, and features artwork by 17 conCheryl Derricotte is one of over a dozen artists featured. temporary artists and collectives who lived in California from the Gold Rush to the Reconstruction period following the Civil War. Black Gold includes never-before-seen commissions by Akea Brionne, Demetri Broxton, Adrian L. Burrell, Adam Davis, Cheryl Derricotte, Mildred Howard, Tiff Massey, Umar Rashid, Trina Michelle Robinson, Bryan Keith Thomas, and Cosmo Whyte. New commissions explore themes of African American resilience during a pivotal era in the American West, including the fight for legal rights within the “free” state of California, the successes of early Black entrepreneurs and the experiences of African American Army regiments known as the Buffalo Soldiers. The exhibition also features recent works by Carla Edwards, Isaac Julien, Alison Saar, and Hank Willis Thomas. The exhibition is presented by FOR-SITE, a nonprofit organization dedicated to the cultural arts, and curated by Cheryl Haines, the nonprofit’s founding executive director. “Black Gold is a collaborative effort that brings together the work of an array of artists, thinkers, and community leaders to reveal narratives that are historically significant and continue to resonate today,” Haines said in a press release. “I am thrilled to shed light on this important part of California’s story.” The exhibition remains on view through November 2. Admission is free. Fort Point National Historic Site is located 201 Marine Drive in San Francisco. For more information, visit www.for-site.org.

articles.text: Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” festival returns on November 7, featuring hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. Running through January 25, 2026, the family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. “Glowfari” displays at Oakland Zoo.

Combine that with the high adventure of Indiana Jones in quest of the Holy Grail. Add the religious visions of the Good Friday spell with its magic, and the exquisite architecture of Santa Chappelle in Paris. All of these are present in Richard Wagner’s opera Parsifal. This all-encompassing opera was the feature of San Francisco Opera performance on Saturday afternoon. The name Richard Wagner arouses a mass of contradictions. He was, himself a man of immense contradiction. So is his music. Both provoked fist fights and physical confrontations, controversy and genetic debate. His very ethnicity has been debated. All of these things are ongoing since his mysterious death in 1883. But the controversy of the subject of Parsifal began much earlier. In literature, it goes back to around 1180 with a romance written by Chretien de Troyes. In legend, it is a central part of King Arthur and his Knights of the round table. The quest for eternal life and effective healing powers have always been elusive. The Nazis thrust these principles to the very forefront of their regime. The story of Parsifal has many detours. Wagner’s operatic version of this story takes five hours and has more turns than the Prix de Monte Carlo. Each listener is welcomed to make a personal interpretation as wished. That’s how elusive the story is. The San Francisco Opera presentation was multifaceted. From the outset I thought that the performance was going to be a dreadful bore of five hours. Despite the strange configurations of the music, the prelude that opens the opera had no magic. The acting was as if in slow motion. I began to think: how is it possible to move so slowly? Things got much better in the second act. All of the singers were in good voice, and they had smooth, rich voices. As is the case these days, the diction was poor, but the spectacle began to unfold. The audience was encouraged to watch and to experience the events. Wagner’s music by itself is a thing of wonder. Saturday, November 8, 3:00 p.m. Ravel’s Complete Solo Piano Works To celebrate the 150th birthday of French composer Maurice Ravel, renowned pianist Dr. Gwendolyn Mok has gathered a group of pianists to perform the complete repertoire of Ravel’s solo piano works at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The 13 pianists come mostly from the Bay Area, with guests from Toronto and Tokyo. They include Silicon Valley engineers, public relations professionals, lawyers, etc. Many have competed in prestigious international piano competitions for amateur pianists and are top prize winners. Note that the organizer will donate proceeds from the event to a major international charity. Get tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6716987. Saturday, November 15, 3:00 p.m. Friends of Ethnic Art Lecture San Francisco Friends of Ethnic Art present an illustrated talk on African Beads by Herbert M. (Skip) Cole, professor emeritus, UCSB. African beads are Sacred and Secular, Symbolic and Sexy: also used as money, medicine, clothing and to show power. Illustrated by slides of people and their beadwork, the talk will explore varied types of beads, their contexts, uses, meanings and aesthetic quality among many African people in different parts of the continent. Bead collectors are encouraged to bring examples to share/discuss. Admission is free and the talk will be followed by a brief wine and snacks reception. Sunday, November 16, 4:00 p.m. Rami Bar-Niv Piano-Solo Recital Internationally renowned Israeli concert pianist, Mr. BarNiv will offer a unique program entitled Rhapsody in Blue and White, to include works by J. S. Bach, W. A. Mozart, JJ Hollingsworth, Frédéric Chopin, George Gershwin, and one composition of his own, based on three Hebrew songs, which gives the solo concert its name. The concert will conclude with BarNiv’s arrangement of Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue, and light refreshments will be available. Advance tickets are at https:// ww.brownpapertickets.com/e/6725302. Thursday, November 20, 7:00 p.m. Miss Maybell & her Ragtime Romeos Get your vintage groove on for this light-hearted, entertaining evening of vintage Jazz, Blues, and Ragtime music. Miss Maybell and her husband Charlie Judkins give new life to songs created over 100 years ago and rescued from old 78 rpm records and antique sheet music. The concert will also feature Marty Eggers on bass and Don Neely, founder of SF’s Royal Society Jazz Orchestra, on clarinet & saxophone. articles.text: The group usually tours Mountain View Cemetery the week of Halloween, and this year’s cemetery walk was planned for October 29. But last Wednesday wasn’t too soon to get in the spirit. With so many “spooktacular” decorations around central Piedmont, the walkers decided to make this week’s route a Halloween house tour. Forty-six walkers, plus one loyal K-9 friend, gathered at the Exedra for the start. Before setting out, they heard a short history of Halloween. The holiday traces back more than 2,000 years to the Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in), celebrated in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom and northern France. The Celts marked Nov. 1 as the new year, the end of harvest, and the beginning of the dark winter season associated with death. They believed that on the night before, Oct. 31, the boundary between the living and the dead blurred and spirits could return to earth. To protect themselves, they lit bonfires and wore costumes made of animal heads and skins. When the Romans conquered Celtic lands, they blended their traditions with Samhain. By the eighth century, Pope Gregory III had declared Nov. 1 All Saints Day, and the evening before became All Hallows Eve—later Halloween. In America, the holiday grew after 19th-century Irish and Scottish immigration, evolving into trick-or-treating, carved pumpkins and costumes. At Highland and Sierra Avenue they spotted their first ghostly figure in a front yard. Down and back up Hazel Lane, a giant spider clung to a house, and on Requa Road they came to a Universal Studios-worthy scene filled with skeletons and lights. It was worthy of a group photo— and a few Halloween facts. Halloween is now the second-largest commercial holiday in the U.S., trailing only Christmas. Americans spent about $950 billion on Christmas in 2023, while 2025 Halloween spending is projected at $13.1 billion—$4.3 billion on costumes, $3.9 billion on candy, and $4.2 billion on decorations. Walkers have Halloween on their minds By Dick Carter The group usually tours Mountain View Cemetery the week of Halloween, and this year’s cemetery walk was planned for October 29. But last Wednesday wasn’t too soon to get in the spirit. With so many “spooktacular” decorations around central Piedmont, the walkers decided to make this week’s route a Halloween house tour. Forty-six walkers, plus one loyal K-9 friend, gathered at the Exedra for the start. Before setting out, they heard a short history of Halloween. The holiday traces back more than 2,000 years to the Celtic festival of Samhain (pronounced sow-in), celebrated in what is now Ireland, the United Kingdom and northern France. The Celts marked Nov. 1 as the new year, the end of harvest, and the beginning of the dark winter season associated with death. They believed that on the night before, Oct. 31, the boundary between the living and the dead blurred and spirits could return to earth. To protect themselves, they lit bonfires and wore costumes made of animal heads and skins. When the Romans conquered Celtic lands, they blended their traditions with Samhain. By the eighth century, Pope Gregory III had declared Nov. 1 All Saints Day, and the evening before became All Hallows Eve—later Halloween. In America, the holiday grew after 19th-century Irish and Scottish immigration, evolving into trick-or-treating, carved pumpkins and costumes. At Highland and Sierra Avenue they spotted their first ghostly figure in a front yard. Down and back up Hazel Lane, a giant spider clung to a house, and on Requa Road they came to a Universal Studios-worthy scene filled with skeletons and lights. It was worthy of a group photo— and a few Halloween facts. Halloween is now the second-largest commercial holiday in the U.S., trailing only Christmas. Americans spent about $950 billion on Christmas in 2023, while 2025 Halloween spending is projected at $13.1 billion—$4.3 billion on costumes, $3.9 billion on candy, and $4.2 billion on decorations. A good share of that seemed to be displayed right there on Requa. From Requa the group retraced its steps to Highland and continued to Wildwood Avenue. Burgundy leaves still clung to the maples lining the street, giving it a warm autumn glow. Ghosts hung from balconies, and a tower of skulls guarded one yard. Everyone was glad no small children were along for this stretch—all the walkers this week were comfortably over six. A real squirrel added comic relief, happily chewing a pile of miniature pumpkins. On Crocker Avenue, just before Lincoln, another highlight appeared: a human skeleton walking a skeleton dog. They continued down Lincoln, passing Piedmont Mayor Betsy Andersen’s festively decorated home. Marigolds in her yard prompted a note that these bright flowers are symbols of Día de Muertos—their color and scent said to guide spirits home. At Sheridan and Caperton Avenues, a lone skeleton rested peacefully against a tree. From there the group began its return to the city center. But at longtime walker June Yee’s suggestion, they detoured up Mountain and Craig Avenues to see one of the morning’s most creative displays: six small witches standing in a circle around a steaming cauldron. Water vapor rose in curls, evoking Auguste Rodin’s sculpture The Burghers of Calais. After that stop, the walkers returned down Highland and continued along Vista Avenue past City Hall and the Corey Reich Tennis Center to Hillside and Magnolia Avenues. Outside the Recreation Center they admired another towering skeleton and a front yard full of Halloween decorations. The Rec Department will host its “Trick or Tasty Treat” event there on Halloween. Before wrapping up, the group peeked at the nearly completed community pool—a final treat at the end of a walk that mixed local color, holiday lore and good company. Walking on Wednesdays meets each week at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra, at Highland and Magnolia Avenues. All are welcome and there is no cost. New walkers and friendly dogs are encouraged. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Portugal, though small in size, is one of the world’s most diverse and distinctive wine-producing countries. With more than 250 indigenous grape varieties—many found nowhere else on earth—Portugal offers an extraordinary range of styles, from crisp, mineral-driven whites to rich, complex reds and world-famous fortified wines. Its winemaking tradition dates back over two millennia, shaped by Roman settlers, monastic orders, and generations of families who continue to craft wines deeply rooted in their regions. Portugal’s geography and climate create a natural tapestry for viticulture. The cool, green northwest is home to Vinho Verde, a refreshing, lightly effervescent white that captures the Atlantic’s maritime influence. Moving inland, the Douro Valley, one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world, produces powerful red table wines and the iconic Port—a fortified wine known for its depth, sweetness, and aging potential. To the south, the Alentejo region contrasts with rolling plains and hot, dry summers that yield bold, fruit-forward reds and smooth, approachable whites. Beyond these famous regions, Portugal’s charm lies in its variety. The Dão offers elegant, structured reds from the Touriga Nacional grape, while the Bairrada region is known for its robust wines made from the Baga variety. Even the volcanic Azores and Madeira islands contribute unique expressions—Madeira itself being another legendary fortified wine prized for its longevity and complexity. Modern Portuguese winemakers have skillfully blended innovation with respect for tradition. Today, Portugal stands at the intersection of authenticity and contemporary appeal, producing wines that combine old-world character with exceptional value. Whether enjoyed as an introduction to Europe’s lesser-known treasures or as a study in terroir and heritage, the wines of Portugal offer a captivating journey through history, landscape, and culture—one glass at a time. I recently had the opportunity to attend a master class and large general tasting of Portuguese wines and ports at the Port Wine Fest in San Francisco on Sept. 30. The range of excellent wines was impressive and I was astounded by the number of grape varieties I had never heard of. The world of Portuguese wine is largely unexplored by the American consumer. My colleagues and I made our way through the tasting searching for the hidden gems. The following wines were the most memorable and deserve the effort to search them out. They are the cream of the crop. The Port wine Fest in San Francisco

KILIMANJARO, October 2016 In honor of Piedmonter Bill Baringer climbing to the top of the highest mountain on each continent, the Post is re-running the articles about each of his climbs, originally published in 2020. The list of the top spots on each continent is called the Seven Summits, which Baringer completed on October 3, 2025 when he submitted Carstensz Pyramid Piedmont’s Bill Baringer, has quietly has climbed the highest mountain peak on each of the seven continents. In late 2016 he embarked on a three-year quest to reach the top of the highest mountain on each of the world’s seven continents before his 60th birthday. His quest clearly was not for the faint-hearted. First on his list of major peaks was Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania; at 19,340 feet, it is Africa’s Local Tanzanian law dictates the only way to summit Kilimanjaro is with a guided travel group. Known throughout the world, the majestic mountain is a popular destination for as many as 30,000 people in any given year. On his first climb, Baringer talked his wife, Cynthia, into joining him. And although it is an easier ascent than some of other major peaks, something can always go wrong. An experienced climber they met on the climb developed optic edema while at the summit, in which her optic nerve became swollen due to altitude pressure. She lost her sight for 24 hours until the swelling went down. The Baringers chose an eightday route from Lemosho, involving 43 miles of hiking and time to acclimatize on the climb. Kilimanjaro is the largest free-standing mountain in the world, making it visually dramatic by land and by air. The trip traverses through alpine desert, moorland, rainforest, lava fields and finally into arctic zones. The ascent of Kilimanjaro began at Lemosho Gate. In the photo Cynthia Baringer is shown surrounded by porters and guides. This mountain creates its own weather, and despite being just three degrees latitude south of the equator, has glaciers on the upper parts of the mountain. Baringer confirmed that due to global warming, the glaciers are melting rapidly, but are still there for the moment. Becoming acclimated to altitude is the main battle with climbing. Thus, hiking slowly to a new height is better than racing up and then resting. The guides constantly told the hikers to slow down, “polepole” (pronounced “POH-lay”), meaning “slowly” in Swahili. But their exhortations didn’t sit well with Baringer. “It is truly challenging for me to walk at what was likely 1 mph. So, I tried juggling rocks while walking, to keep myself entertained,” he said with a grin. The day of reaching the summit is usually the hardest climb, Cynthia and Bill Baringer, still in his hiking shorts, stop for a photo at a base camp at an elevation of 12,600 feet. Most of the trip is a gradual incline, but the trail does get steep at times. articles.text: With bags strapped onto the front and back of dual kayaks and food and tents piled into a small motorboat, they pushed off into the cold water for a long paddle. When they finally reached the campsite, they set up their tents and changed into their swimwear, spending the rest of the day together exploring the shore, building sand castles, wading in the water, and playing Uno. The Scouts waited for darkness to fall so that they could see the famed bioluminescence of Tomales Bay. The bioluminescence comes from single-celled organisms called dinoflagellates. This phenomenon occurs during the summer, becoming visible to the human eye when agitated in the dark of the night. At first it was difficult to see the bioluminescence, but sounds of excitement filled the air as the water around their paddles lit up with sparkles and swirls. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors marked their 29th anniversary in lively style on Sept. 24, gathering more than 60 members and guests at the Piedmont Community Hall for a day filled with learning, laughter, and local connection. The celebration began with the group’s regular monthly business meeting, followed by a special presentation from Clars Auctions. Senior Vice President Deric Torres and Director of Marketing Talesa Eugenio shared insights into what makes items most valuable at auction. The talk turned into a local version of “Antiques Roadshow” as six members took the stage to showcase family treasures — from antique paintings and pottery to a pair of silver swords and even a photo of a stately grandfather clock. Lunches from Joaquin Deli in San Leandro added to the festivities, and attendees enjoyed a presentation on white-collar crime by FBI Agent Michael Rolden, introduced by Piedmont’s new Police Chief Frederick Shavies. Rolden offered practical advice for preventing fraud and encouraged residents to report online scams at www.ic3.gov. articles.text: You don’t have to wait until selling to make the most of your home. Your spare room is an opportunity to elevate your home’s function and appeal. With a little creativity—and a yearly declutter—it can shift from forgotten storage to a space that improve your space. While it is easy to let spare rooms become storage spaces, a yearly declutter can breathe new life into your home. Instead of filling unused rooms with forgotten belongings, clear the clutter and give the space a purpose. You can sell, consign, or donate items to make the process simpler. Once you’ve cleared out the excess, here are five creative ideas to inspire your transformation: 1. Build a Home Library For book lovers, nothing compares to having a dedicated reading retreat. Line the walls with shelves, add a cozy armchair or loveseat, and soften the atmosphere with warm lighting, pillows, and a throw blanket. This creates a quiet corner perfect for escaping into your favorite stories. 2. Create a Multi-Use Room If you can’t decide on one purpose, make the room adaptable. A Murphy bed, wall-mounted desk, or modular furniture can transform the space throughout the day—guest room by night, office by day, and even a small home gym when needed. Hidden storage and collapsible bins keep it tidy and functional. 3. Design a Music Lounge Turn your extra room into a sanctuary for sound. Add a quality speaker system or vintage record player, cozy seating, and personal touches like instruments, framed album covers, or posters. Whether you’re winding down with mellow tunes or enjoying a lively jam session, this room will radiate personality. 4. Arrange an Entertainment Space Make your spare room the ultimate hangout zone. A projector or large screen sets the stage for movie nights, while bean bags or a sectional keep things comfortable. Add shelving for games, a snack cart, or colorful lighting to create a fun, welcoming atmosphere for family and friends. 5. Create a Relaxation Escape Sometimes, the most valuable transformation is into a serene retreat. Keep the space clutter-free and soothing with simple décor, soft lighting, a diffuser, and comfortable seating. This can be your go-to spot for meditation, journaling, or simply recharging away from the bustle of everyday life. Transform your spare room: from storage to stylish living You don’t have to wait until selling to make the most of your home. By Debbi DiMaggio Your spare room is an opportunity to elevate your home’s function and appeal. With a little creativity—and a yearly declutter—it can shift from forgotten storage to a space that improve your space. While it is easy to let spare rooms become storage spaces, a yearly declutter can breathe new life into your home. Instead of filling unused rooms with forgotten belongings, clear the clutter and give the space a purpose. You can sell, consign, or donate items to make the process simpler. Once you’ve cleared out the excess, here are five creative ideas to inspire your transformation: 1. Build a Home Library For book lovers, nothing compares to having a dedicated reading retreat. Line the walls with shelves, add a cozy armchair or loveseat, and soften the atmosphere with warm lighting, pillows, and a throw blanket. This creates a quiet corner perfect for escaping into your favorite stories. 2. Create a Multi-Use Room If you can’t decide on one purpose, make the room adaptable. A Murphy bed, wall-mounted desk, or modular furniture can transform the space throughout the day—guest room by night, office by day, and even a small home gym when needed. Hidden storage and collapsible bins keep it tidy and functional. 3. Design a Music Lounge Turn your extra room into a sanctuary for sound. Add a quality speaker system or vintage record player, cozy seating, and personal touches like instruments, framed album covers, or posters. Whether you’re winding down with mellow tunes or enjoying a lively jam session, this room will radiate personality. 4. Arrange an Entertainment Space Make your spare room the ultimate hangout zone. A projector or large screen sets the stage for movie nights, while bean bags or a sectional keep things comfortable. Add shelving for games, a snack cart, or colorful lighting to create a fun, welcoming atmosphere for family and friends. 5. Create a Relaxation Escape Sometimes, the most valuable transformation is into a serene retreat. Keep the space clutter-free and soothing with simple décor, soft lighting, a diffuser, and comfortable seating. This can be your go-to spot for meditation, journaling, or simply recharging away from the bustle of everyday life. In the Bay Area, education isn’t just for the young. More adults over 50 are joining creative learning communities to stay sharp, connected, and purposeful. Research shows that continued learning later in life boosts cognitive health, reduces isolation, and can even extend longevity. For many, though, the classroom now looks a bit different — filled not with textbooks and tests, but with laughter, storytelling, and the rhythm of tap shoes. At Oakland’s Stagebridge, one of the nation’s first performing arts programs for older adults, students meet weekly to study acting, music, and movement. The focus isn’t applause, but growth. “We learn lines, we forget them, we laugh, and we try again,” says one participant. “That’s life practice, not just acting practice.” Experts point to neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to form new connections at any age, as the key to staying mentally agile and emotionally resilient. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Patty Brown passed away peacefully at home on September 13, 2025. Born Patricia DeWitt Brown on July 22, 1933 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Mae Louise Coolidge and James Quinne DeWitt Sr. Patty spent most of her life residing in the Bay Area and Piedmont except for the last 15 years when she moved to San Diego to be close to her daughters and their families. A beacon of kindness, she touched the lives of all who knew her. Patty spent several years in Hawaii where she learned to surf and discovered a lifelong passion for the islands. Her adventurous spirit led her to water-ski, snowski, and travel the world. Patty enjoyed an early career as a dental assistant before raising her family and eventually teaching Preschool. She was an enthusiastic reader, active member of her community, member of the Town & Gown Club of Berkeley, and a devoted family member and loyal friend. Patricia is survived by her daughters Victoria Moats (Thomas) and Elizabeth Brown (Samisoni) and five grandchildren, Jessica Moats, Ryan Moats, Kenny Moats, Noah Molimoli and Olivia Molimoli, who will forever carry her memory in their hearts. She will be deeply missed, but her legacy of love and kindness will continue to inspire and touch all who had the privilege of knowing her. articles.text: Jim Smith, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away peacefully in Oakland on September 19, 2025. He was 82. Jim was an accomplished businessman with unparalleled wit and a heart of gold. He was “the last of the lion kings,” as a dear friend reflected, “and a person who had an enormous impact on everyone with whom he came into contact, consistently adding humor and nuance to our lives.” He loved Henny Youngman, the British-born American comedian and musician famous for his mastery of the “one-liner” – and that was Jim! Born James Richard Smith in 1943 to Robert and Mildred Smith in Portland, Oregon, he grew up there with his sister Barbara. He did well academically and excelled at basketball from an early age. He was a star at Wilson High School where his team won the all-city and state championships. Jim’s basketball ability benefitted from his height of 6’8” and a rigorous practice schedule that grew into the steadfast and tenacious work ethic for which he was later known. Smith was the focal point of Southern Methodist University’s offense where he was a forward, becoming Co-Captain of the team in his third varsity season. With Smith in tow, the Mustangs captured the 1965 Southwest Conference Championship and reached the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16. Jim was inducted into the Portland Interscholastic League Hall of Fame in 2022. In 1960, he met his high school sweetheart, Sharon. Together, they went on to SMU where he had a full basketball scholarship and studied marketing and finance. Upon graduation from college, the two were married in Lake Oswego, Oregon. They then drove across the country in he was able to coach them in basketball and little league baseball. This enthusiasm found him spearheading the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation. Jim was endlessly proud of the good men his sons have become and the wonderful families they have created. He loved being ‘Poppy’ to his grandchildren, never failing to let each one of them know how much they meant to him - in between ribbing them with a good joke, that ultimately served to shape their sensibilities in navigating life’s adventures. One of the great landscapes of Jim’s life was Claremont Country Club. He revered every aspect of the Club’s traditions, though it was the members and the staff that he treasured most. Jim was President during a critical period of historic preservation that helped to define the experience and beauty of the Club today. When not at the Club he enjoyed entertaining at their bungalow in St. Helena, CA. He had a full circle of friendships, keeping up with people from all over the world. This truly was his joy. His memory will live on in the hearts of all those who knew and loved him. Jim is survived by his wife of 60 years, Sharon Smith, children Jeff (AnnMarie) Smith, and Jamie (Melinda) Smith, and seven grandchildren: Carter, Brady, Alyssa, Andrew, Ashley, Charlie and Caroline. He also played an important role in many extended family member’s lives, including Brian and Noah Berry and all of his dear nieces and nephews, and great nieces and nephews. Friends and Family are invited to the Celebration of Life for Jim on November 2, 2025 at 2:00 pm. Donations to the Claremont Country Club Oak Tree Foundation, Dumbarton Oaks Park Conservancy, or a charity of your choice, are greatly appreciated. The group setting of a hike tends to create lifelong friends with people from literally all over the world. Baringer made an impression on a fellow hiker from Denmark, Sofie Dyhr Meister, the mother of two boys, Marcus and Nicklas, all of whom made it to the summit. When he saw her two sons at the top, he said, “Wow, there are my two heroes.” “I was very proud that a stranger had taken notice of their accomplishment,” she recently told the Post. “I will never forget those kind words.” Baringer admitted that he has gotten hooked on what he describes as “Type 2 Fun,” a cycle of climbing. He describes it in chronological order. “First you show up to base camp, you survive miserable conditions, then you summit, and swear off climbing again. As the days and weeks pass, he demonstrates an extraordinary ability to adapt to his isolation and potentially lethal circumstances. He searches the many damaged hallways and crumbling rooms and with found binoculars watches the street below for the soldiers who are relentlessly searching for those Jews who are still hidden in the devastation.
